client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Everything just feels kind of gray and heavy, like I go through the motions of my day but nothing feels meaningful or enjoyable anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because she's still gone no matter what I say in here.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — what you're describing, that gray, heavy feeling where the color seems to drain out of everyday life, makes complete sense as part of grief, and I hear in your voice how much you're carrying right now. You're absolutely right that talking won't bring her back, and I want to honor that truth rather than dismiss it. What we *can* do together is help you find a way to carry this loss without it swallowing everything that still matters to you — and that's worth something, even if it doesn't feel that way yet.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, I really do, but I guess I'm just not sure what "carrying it without it swallowing everything" even looks like in practice. Like, she was the one person who actually got me, who I could call when things felt too heavy, and now that's just... gone. I don't know how you move forward from something like that without it feeling like you're somehow leaving her behind.
therapist: That fear of moving forward feeling like abandonment is one of the most painful parts of grief, and the tension in your voice tells me this isn't just a passing thought — it's something you're genuinely wrestling with. But I want to gently offer a different perspective: moving forward doesn't mean leaving her behind, it can actually mean carrying *her* with you — the way she understood you, what she taught you about feeling seen, the parts of yourself that grew because she was in your life. What if honoring her looked less like staying still in the pain, and more like learning to be, over time, some of what she was for you — that steady, understanding presence — for yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it feels almost too neat, like a way of wrapping something messy in a bow. She was the one person who really got me without me having to explain myself, and I don't know how I'm supposed to become that for myself when I could barely even recognize what I was feeling until she named it for me. It's like you're asking me to be my own translator when I don't even speak the language yet.
therapist: You're speaking quickly and there's a real urgency in what you're saying — and you're right to push back, because that *was* too neat, and you deserved honesty more than a tidy reframe. What you're describing — losing the person who helped you understand yourself before you even had the words — is a profound kind of loss that goes beyond missing someone, it's like losing a part of your own inner compass. And I don't want to rush past that; maybe right now the work isn't about becoming your own translator, but simply about slowing down enough together, here, to start learning that language one word at a time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate that you didn't just try to wrap it up with something hopeful-sounding, because I think that's what I usually get and it just makes me feel more alone somehow. But I'm not sure I even know what "slowing down" looks like — like, my brain doesn't really have an off switch, and sitting in the quiet with this grief just feels like drowning, not learning. I guess I'm scared that if we go slow, I'll just be stuck in the pain longer without it actually going anywhere.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, pitched high, like you're trying to stay just ahead of something — tells me that fear of drowning isn't abstract, it's right here with you right now. And that fear makes complete sense: "slowing down" shouldn't mean sitting alone in a flood, and I want to be clear that's not what I'm asking of you. What if slowing down actually means the opposite of being stuck — not staring into the grief alone, but gradually, with support, learning to touch the edges of it without it pulling you under completely?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but I honestly don't know what "touching the edges" even looks like in practice. Like, every time I get close to thinking about how lonely I've been since my mom died, it doesn't feel like edges — it just feels like the whole thing crashes in at once. And I guess I'm scared that if I start, I won't be able to stop it.
therapist: I notice you mentioned your mom just now — and I want to make sure I'm understanding, because that feels significant, and I don't want to move past it too quickly. The fear you're describing, that once you open the door it all floods in at once with no way to stop it, is one of the most common and most real fears in grief, and it makes complete sense that your mind has been working hard to keep that door closed. What I want you to know is that part of our work together is specifically about building a kind of container first — so that when we do approach those feelings, you're not facing that flood alone and without a way back to solid ground.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, that there's some way to approach it without just completely falling apart. But honestly, I've spent so long keeping that door shut that I'm not even sure I know how to start building whatever that container is supposed to be. It just feels like something you're saying to reassure me, and I don't know if it actually works that way in real life.
therapist: Your voice is soft right now, almost careful, like you're holding something fragile — and I think that's worth naming, because it tells me this isn't skepticism for its own sake, it's a kind of exhausted hoping that's been disappointed before. You're right to ask me to be concrete rather than reassuring, so here's what I actually mean: building a container starts with something as small as what's happening right now — you naming the fear, me hearing it, and nothing catastrophic happening as a result. That *is* the container, in its earliest form — and you've already begun it, even if it doesn't feel that way yet.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, that just naming something out loud and having someone not flinch is actually meaningful. But I keep thinking, okay, nothing catastrophic happened here, in this room, but that's kind of a controlled environment, isn't it? Out there, when I've let my guard down with people I actually know, it hasn't gone the same way, and that's the gap I don't know how to cross.
therapist: There's something urgent and almost raw in the way you're saying this — like this isn't a hypothetical fear, it's something you've lived, where you reached out and it didn't go the way it needed to. That gap you're describing, between being safe here and being safe *out there*, is real and it matters, and I don't want to pretend this room magically transfers to the rest of your life without work. But I'm curious — when you've let your guard down with people and it hasn't gone well, what happened, and what did you take away about yourself from those moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client:
Yeah, it's not hypothetical at all. There was this person I considered a close friend, and I opened up about how anxious I'd been feeling, how isolated, and they kind of just... went quiet after that. Not immediately, but gradually they stopped reaching out, and I kept telling myself maybe I was too much, maybe I made it weird by being honest about struggling.

What I took away, I guess, is that being vulnerable is basically a way of handing someone a reason to leave. And I know that probably sounds dramatic, but it felt like proof of something I already suspected about myself — that when people really see what's going on inside, they don't actually want to stay around for it.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, pitched high, like the words are trying to keep up with something painful moving through you — tells me this memory still carries a lot of weight, and I want to sit with that for a moment before anything else. What you took away from that experience makes complete sense given what happened, but I want to gently name it as a conclusion your mind drew from one person's limitations, not evidence of a universal truth about you. That friend's silence said something about their capacity to show up — not about whether you are worth showing up for.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, I really do. But it's hard because this wasn't just one person — it feels like a pattern, like every time I've really needed someone, there's been this silence, and at some point you start wondering if the common denominator is you. I guess I'm just not sure I can separate "their limitations" from "something about me" when it keeps happening the same way.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but fast, like you're bracing for something even as you say it — tells me this thought, that you might be the problem, isn't new, and it carries a lot of quiet weight. I want to take that seriously rather than dismiss it, because you're right that patterns deserve more than "it was just them" — but I'd also gently ask: is it possible that what's consistent across these silences isn't something broken in you, but rather that you've been bringing your realest self to people who didn't have the capacity to meet you there? That's not a flaw in you — that might actually be a painful mismatch between your depth and who you've had access to.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That's... a really kind way to frame it, and part of me wants to hold onto it. But I also wonder if I'm just telling myself a flattering story, you know? Like, maybe "they couldn't meet me where I was" is just a nicer way of saying I'm too much, or too intense, or I expect things people can't actually give.
therapist: There's something striking happening right now — your words are questioning and uncertain, but your voice is tight and quick, like part of you is working hard to talk yourself out of something that almost felt safe to believe. The question you're asking — "am I just telling myself a flattering story?" — is actually a really important CBT question, so let's take it seriously: what would the *evidence* need to look like for you to know the difference between a self-protective story and an accurate one? Because "I'm too much" is also a story, and it's worth asking which one has more actual proof behind it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
